articles.title: What is MCP?
articles.summary: An open protocol for connecting Claude Code to databases, browsers, APIs, and repositories without leaving the session

blocks.content: MCP (Model Context Protocol) standardizes how language models connect to external systems. Claude Code uses it to access tools beyond the local filesystem — securely, declaratively, and without interrupting the workflow.

items.title: 🧩 Extensible by design
items.body: Any tool with an MCP server integrates the same way — databases, cloud services, internal APIs, automated browsers.

items.title: 🔒 Credentials under control
items.body: The three scopes let you decide precisely which credentials the team shares and which stay personal, without mixing them.

items.title: ⚡ Tool Search: no overhead
items.body: Claude Code loads tool definitions on demand, not all at once. Minimal impact on the context window even with several servers connected.

items.label: Tool Search loads a tool's schema right when it's about to be invoked, not all of them upfront
scopes to control each server's visibility
impact on the context window as more connected servers are added (per official docs — no exact figure published)

articles.title: Adding servers
articles.summary: Commands to register MCP servers across different scopes and transports

blocks.content: claude mcp add playwright -- npx -y @playwright/mcp --headless
claude mcp add --transport http github https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp
claude mcp add -e API_KEY=xxx -e DB_URL=yyy myserver -- npx my-server
Useful for complex configurations with multiple arguments:
claude mcp add-json postgres '{"command":"npx","args":["-y","@mcp/postgres"],"env":{"DB":"$DATABASE_URL"}}'

claude mcp add --scope project shared-db -- npx @mcp/postgres
claude mcp add --scope user brave -- npx @brave/brave-search-mcp-server
claude mcp add --scope local secret-tool -- npx my-private-server

articles.title: Managing servers
articles.summary: List, inspect, and remove registered MCP servers

blocks.content:
# List all servers and their status
claude mcp list

# Inspect a specific server (config + connection status)
claude mcp get playwright

# Remove a server
claude mcp remove playwright

# Remove from a specific scope (if it exists in several)
claude mcp remove --scope project playwright

rows: Adds a stdio server to the local scope
Useful for configs with multiple args
Inspects a server's config and status
Imports to local scope by default

articles.title: In-session commands
articles.summary: The /mcp command for managing servers during an interactive session

blocks.content:
# Open the MCP management panel (also handles OAuth 2.1)
/mcp

# Enable / disable a server for this session
/mcp enable playwright
/mcp disable playwright

# Enable / disable all
/mcp enable all
/mcp disable all
The `/mcp` command also drives the OAuth 2.1 flow for remote servers that require authentication.
claude mcp add-from-claude-desktop
Useful for migrating an existing Claude.app configuration. Imports to local scope by default. Imported servers can be moved to a different scope afterward.

articles.title: Where each server lives
articles.summary: The three scopes determine who can see an MCP server and in which projects it's available

blocks.content: The scope determines who can see an MCP server and in which projects it's available. Choosing it correctly avoids leaking credentials to the team or forcing every developer to reconfigure the same thing.
If the same server name is defined in more than one scope, the resolution order is: **local → project → user** (first one wins).
You only, this project only. The default scope when nothing is specified. Ideal for experimenting with a new server or when the credentials are yours, not the team's.

# --scope local is implicit
claude mcp add playwright -- npx -y @playwright/mcp --headless

# With personal credentials
claude mcp add -e PERSONAL_TOKEN=$MY_TOKEN internal-tool -- npx my-tool
The whole team, in this project. Stored in `.mcp.json` and versioned with Git. Credentials go in as `$VAR` references, never as literal values.

# Team server: stored in .mcp.json and committed
claude mcp add --scope project github --transport http https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp

# With an environment variable reference (the real value isn't committed)
claude mcp add --scope project -e DB_URL=$DATABASE_URL postgres -- npx @mcp/postgres

# Each team dev has their own DATABASE_URL variable
# The server is shared, the credentials aren't
You only, across all your projects. Personal tools you always use, regardless of the project.

# Available across all your projects
claude mcp add --scope user brave-search -- npx -y @brave/brave-search-mcp-server

# Personal productivity tools
claude mcp add --scope user obsidian -- npx @obsidian/mcp-server
claude mcp add --scope user linear -- npx @linear/mcp-server

articles.title: Lazy loading of tools
articles.summary: How Claude Code loads tool definitions on demand to reduce context consumption

subsections.title: The problem with traditional MCP clients

blocks.content: Most MCP clients load every tool definition from every server at the start of each session. Connecting 5 servers with 20 tools each injects the schemas of all 100 tools into the context — regardless of whether they'll be used. This can consume tens of thousands of tokens just for definitions.

left.label: 🐌 Other MCP clients
items: 100% of definitions loaded at startup
All schemas in context from the very first message
Consumption grows linearly with each added server
10 servers = saturated context before starting

right.label: ⚡ Claude Code with Tool Search
items: Only the schema of the tools that will actually be invoked gets loaded
Minimal impact on the context window (per official docs, no exact figure published)
Multiple servers can be connected without saturating the window
Token cost scales much less with the number of servers

items.title: Registering available servers
items.description: When the session starts, Claude Code registers the connected servers but doesn't load their tools. It only knows they exist.

items.title: On-demand search
items.description: When the task requires a specific capability, Claude Code searches among the available servers for one that can cover it — similar to a semantic search over the server's metadata.

items.title: Loading the specific schema
items.description: Only the schema of the tool about to be invoked gets loaded. The rest of the tools from the same server and from other servers stay out of the context.

items.title: Invocation and result
items.description: The tool is invoked with the correct parameters and the result is integrated into the context. The schema can be unloaded from the context afterward if it's no longer needed.

articles.title: The .mcp.json file
articles.summary: The shared MCP server configuration for teams lives in .mcp.json at the project root

blocks.label: .mcp.json

blocks.content: Environment variables can be used in these fields:

items.title: ✅ Allowed
items.body: command, args (any element in the array), url, headers (values), env (values). Supported syntax: $VAR and ${VAR}.

items.title: ❌ Forbidden
items.body: Pasting tokens directly into .mcp.json. Committing .mcp.json with hardcoded secrets. Using literal sensitive values in headers.

blocks.label: With custom headers and variables

blocks.content: If a referenced variable doesn't exist when the session starts, Claude Code reports a missing-variable warning (visible in `claude mcp list`) and uses the literal unexpanded text `${VAR}` as-is — it doesn't omit it or replace it with an empty string. In practice, this almost always makes the connection fail (for example, a URL with a literal `${VAR}` is invalid).

rows: SQL queries, schema inspection, explain plans.
Issues, PRs, repos, code search. HTTP + OAuth.
Real-time web search from the session.
Access to specific directories outside the project.

articles.title: Structured error responses
articles.summary: MCP's isError flag is just the starting point. Categorizing the error and marking whether it's retryable is what lets the agent make the correct recovery decision.

blocks.content: MCP defines an isError: true flag so a server can tell the client that a tool call failed, instead of returning a raw exception. But that flag alone doesn't tell the agent what to do next: a network timeout, invalid input, a business policy violation, and a denied permission are completely different errors that require completely different responses. A generic message like "Operation failed" forces the agent to guess.

rows: Retry automatically, with backoff if there are several attempts
Invalid date format, missing required field
Fix the parameter and retry with a valid value
Token without sufficient scope, resource outside the allowed root
Don't retry — inform the user or escalate, never keep insisting with the same token
Refund above the policy limit, suspended account
Explain the reason to the user; consider escalating to a human, don't retry

blocks.content: A `business` or `permission` error marked as retryable can make the agent insist on the same action several times without anything changing — it wastes turns and, in the worst case, produces a retry pattern that reads like an agent bug. The `isRetryable` field cuts off that loop at the root.

subsections.title: Access failures vs. valid empty results

blocks.content: A subtle but critical distinction: when a search tool finds nothing, that isn't an error. A lookup_customer that finds no customer with that email succeeded — the correct response is "no results," not a failure. Confusing the two leads to two opposite anti-patterns: treating a legitimate empty result as if it were a failure (and retrying pointlessly), or — worse — having the server return an empty list as a successful response when there was actually a timeout or connection error, hiding the real failure.

rows.value: The search ran correctly; there simply are no matches
Inform the user the record wasn't found, ask for an alternate identifier
{ results: [] } — but there was actually a silenced timeout
The server suppressed the error and disguised it as 'no results'
The agent assumes the customer doesn't exist when the search actually never completed

blocks.content: Design rule: an MCP server should never convert an internal exception into a successful empty result to "simplify" the response. If the search couldn't run, it's isError: true with category transient or permission. If it ran and found nothing, it's isError: false with an empty array. These are semantically distinct states and must remain distinguishable to the agent.

articles.title: What to know before connecting a server
articles.summary: Security considerations, permissions, and best practices for MCP servers

items.title: 🔑 Never hardcode credentials
items.body: .mcp.json gets committed to the repo. Any token included directly stays exposed in the git history forever. Always use $VAR references.

items.title: ⚠️ Prompt injection via tool result
items.body: A compromised MCP server can return content designed to manipulate Claude's behavior. Verify the source of third-party servers before using them in project scope.

items.title: 🌐 HTTP servers: review which domains you allow
items.body: Adding an HTTP server means letting Claude Code send data to that domain. With sandboxing, add the domain to allowedDomains.

items.title: 🔐 OAuth 2.1: least privilege
items.body: OAuth tokens are stored locally. If the token has broad scopes (write access to every repo in an org), configure servers with the least-privilege principle.

blocks.label: Block an entire server
Allow only specific tools
Block only destructive tools

items.title: 🔒 Scope by sensitivity
items.body: Servers with team credentials → project scope (with $VAR references). Personal or experimental credentials → local or user scope.

items.title: ⚡ Start with local scope
items.body: Test the server in local scope first. Once verified it works and exposes nothing sensitive, promote it to project scope for the team.

items.title: 📦 Version without secrets
items.body: Committing .mcp.json standardizes the team's configuration — but only if every sensitive value is a $VAR reference. Document the required variables in the README.

items.title: 🔍 Audit periodically
items.body: claude mcp list shows all servers and their status. Review regularly for obsolete servers or expired credentials.

blocks.content:
**Before adding an MCP server to project scope:**

- Never hardcode tokens or secrets in .mcp.json — always $VAR references.
- Project scope for team servers, local scope for experiments and personal credentials.
- The SSE transport is deprecated — use HTTP with OAuth 2.1 for remote servers.
- Use `deny: ["mcp__server"]` to block entire servers, or `mcp__server__tool` for specific tools.
- With sandboxing active, add the HTTP server's domain to allowedDomains or the server will fail.
- `~/.claude.json` (MCP local/user scope) ≠ `.claude/settings.local.json` (project settings). They're different files.

subsections.title: Tool design: bounded capability, not absolute

blocks.content: The most expensive design mistake in an MCP server isn't a configuration one but a surface-area one: exposing a single tool of absolute capability — a `run_command` that accepts any string and executes it, or undifferentiated read/write access to an entire database — instead of a bounded set of capabilities with an explicit contract. With auto-execute as the default permission, that tool shifts all containment control onto the model, which doesn't know the approval policy of whoever invoked it.

left.label: Absolute-capability tool ❌
items: A single `run_command` or full database access, without distinguishing the operation
The model decides how far to go — the application has no control point
Read and write, or query and delete, share the same approval
Auditing what ran requires parsing the command string after the fact

right.label: Contract-bounded tools ✅
items: Separate capabilities (`check_stock`, `update_stock`, `delete_record`)
Each tool declares its own permission — granular via `mcp__server__tool`
Destructive operations stay in `ask` or `deny` without affecting read operations
The name of the invoked tool is already the audit record

blocks.content: There is no Anthropic-documented native guardrail against recursion or loops inside an MCP server — for example, a tool that internally calls itself again with no stop condition. The only containment mechanisms are operational, not design-level: a per-server timeout (`timeout` field in `.mcp.json`, in milliseconds) and an output-size cap (`MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS`, on the order of 25,000 tokens per call by default). Neither stops a single-step destructive call; they only bound how much time or text an already-occurring failure can consume. Validating the server in a sandbox before production and setting the timeout explicitly isn't optional — it's the only safety net that exists for this case.

blocks.label: Explicit per-server timeout — the only safety net against a loop
